q2.answer: In the single-row SQLite `sync_state` table as `staging_last_saved_id`, in the same database as the staged product rows. Each page's rows and the new `staging_last_saved_id` are written in one SQLite transaction, so the saved position always matches exactly the pages saved, and refetching a page is harmless because rows are upserts.

q3.answer: The client records a watermark (highest committed change_seq) before fetching any page. After the last page it replays `/changes` from the watermark in staging (catch-up) before going live. Pages are read after the watermark, so earlier edits are already in them. Later edits (new low ids, changes, deletes after the page was saved) arrive through the feed, so no gaps are possible.

q5.answer: It is built as a separate staging generation: rows are written under a new generation number beside the live one, with its own watermark, page cursor and catch-up. The live catalogue is untouched while this runs. It becomes the one the app reads when a single transaction sets `live_generation = staging_generation` and `live_cursor_seq = staging_cursor_seq` after catch-up finishes. Old generations are cleaned up afterwards.

q9.answer: During catch-up into staging, an upsert or delete is applied only when the incoming change_seq is at least the stored row's change_seq. A delete of a missing row is a no-op. Page rows are written as upserts. For the live incremental sync, I did not specify a comparison; changes are applied in order, as upserts and deletes by removing the row.

q10.answer: It starts from `live_cursor_seq` stored in SQLite `sync_state`, sent as `after_seq`. It moves forward to the response's `next_seq` in the same transaction that applies that batch of changes, so the cursor and the data never disagree. It does not advance if the batch fails. After a resync it is set from the staging cursor at the swap.

q11.answer: The server reads the products table, filtered by `change_seq > after_seq` using the index on change_seq, ordered by change_seq, limited to 1,000. Each product row holds only its latest version, so the feed shows each changed product's latest state, not its history. Deletes are the soft-delete tombstone rows (`deleted = true`) and appear as entries with `deleted: true`, until the purge job removes them after 7 days.
